summary:
I've been building an intranet dashboard for the small server fleet I run at home — fleet health and an app launcher, deployed via Gitea CI on push. The interesting bit was chasing down a UniFi switch: one port was throwing packet errors at about 0.3% of traffic, another looked "up" at 100Mb but its partner was transmitting literally zero frames for an hour straight. I'd been trusting the controller's own client/port records, which turned out to be unreliable — devices reported "online" for tens of minutes after they'd actually left. Ended up switching to ARP verification and raw byte counters instead of anything the controller claims about connection state.

On the AI infrastructure side, I run a couple of large open models on a single shared GPU (an old Tesla P100) behind a small FastAPI proxy I wrote — Switchboard — that serializes access across four or five different backends so they don't collide and OOM each other. Recent work there was a debugging trail: a "warm" request to one backend was silently adding 10+ seconds because the eviction logic waited for VRAM to settle in a way that never happened for models holding memory persistently. Fixing that cut round-trip latency by roughly two-thirds for the affected model.

I also did a small power-accounting project — logging draw on that GPU box for four months and finally building a dashboard to look at it, rather than letting the CSV pile up unread. Mean draw came out to about 179W, translating to roughly $18/month, which landed right in the middle of what I'd guessed going in. The more useful part was making the dashboard itself honest about its own data: it draws real gaps as gaps instead of interpolating over a period where the logger silently died for two weeks, and it flags staleness instead of pretending everything's fine.

highlights.oneLiner: Fixed a warm-request eviction stall on the shared P100 proxy, cutting round-trip latency about two-thirds
